description: Specific heat capacity, specific latent heat of fusion and vaporisation, and heating curves.
content_html:
Changes of State

Matter can change between three states — solid, liquid and gas. These are physical changes: they are reversible and no new substance is formed. Crucially, mass is conserved during any change of state — the same particles are present before and after; only their arrangement and spacing change.

The key changes of state are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas). Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid at any temperature — the fastest-moving particles at the surface escape as gas. Boiling occurs throughout the entire liquid at a specific temperature when enough energy is supplied. Evaporation causes cooling because the most energetic particles leave, reducing the average kinetic energy of those remaining.

Key Fact

Changes of state are physical, reversible changes that conserve mass. Evaporation occurs at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature. Both transfer particles from liquid to gas state.

Internal Energy

When you heat a substance, you increase its internal energy. Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in the substance. It is important to distinguish between temperature and internal energy: temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, while internal energy includes both kinetic and potential contributions from every particle.

Heating a substance can do one of two things. If the substance remains in the same state, the energy increases the kinetic energy of the particles — they move faster and the temperature rises. If a change of state is occurring, the energy instead increases the potential energy of the particles by breaking the forces between them (or forming them during cooling), and the temperature stays constant during this process.

A heating curve shows temperature on the y-axis against time (or energy supplied) on the x-axis. The graph has sloping sections, where temperature rises (kinetic energy of particles increases), and flat sections (plateaus), where the temperature stays constant while a change of state occurs (potential energy changes as bonds between particles are broken or formed).

The first plateau is at the melting point (solid changing to liquid). The second plateau is at the boiling point (liquid changing to gas). During each plateau, the substance exists as a mixture of two states. The length of each plateau depends on the specific latent heat of the substance for that change of state — a longer plateau means more energy is needed to complete the transition. The gradient of the sloping sections depends on the specific heat capacity — a shallower slope indicates a higher specific heat capacity (more energy per degree).

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity (SHC) quantifies how much energy is needed to heat a given mass of material. Different materials require different amounts of energy for the same temperature rise. Water has a high SHC of 4200 J/(kg °C), meaning it takes a large amount of energy to heat it — which is why it is used in central heating systems and why coastal regions have more moderate climates than inland areas.

The equation linking energy change to temperature change is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in thermal energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C)), and \(\Delta \theta\) is the temperature change (°C). You must be able to rearrange this equation — for example, \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times \Delta \theta}\) or \(\Delta \theta = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times c}\). Always check units before substituting.

Question: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C? (SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

Answer: \(\Delta \theta = 80 - 20 = 60\) °C. \(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504{,}000\) J = 504 kJ.

To investigate the SHC of a metal block: drill two holes in the block — one for a thermometer and one for an electrical immersion heater. Measure the block’s mass using a balance. Record the starting temperature, switch on the heater, and record the energy supplied using a joulemeter and the final temperature when heating is stopped. Rearrange to find \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times \Delta \theta}\). The main source of error is heat lost to the surroundings; wrapping the block in insulating material (lagging) reduces this. This PAG also involves comparing the SHC of water and aluminium.

Key Fact

Specific heat capacity equation: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). SHC is measured in J/(kg °C). Water has a high SHC (4200 J/(kg °C)), requiring a large energy input for a small temperature rise — making it ideal for central heating and thermal energy storage.

Specific Latent Heat

Specific latent heat (SLH) is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature. There is no temperature change during the process — all the energy goes into breaking or forming the intermolecular forces between particles. There are two types:

• Specific latent heat of fusion (\(L_f\)) — the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point (or released when it freezes). For water, \(L_f = 334{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).
• Specific latent heat of vaporisation (\(L_v\)) — the energy needed to change 1 kg from liquid to gas at its boiling point. For water, \(L_v = 2{,}260{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much greater than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because particles must fully overcome the intermolecular forces to become a gas (much more energy is needed than just separating them partially as in melting). The equation relating thermal energy to a change of state is:

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is the thermal energy for the change of state (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg).

Question: How much energy is needed to completely melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (\(L_f\) for water = 334 000 J/kg)

Answer: \(E = m \times L_f = 0.5 \times 334{,}000 = 167{,}000 \text{ J}\) (or 167 kJ). Note: the temperature stays at 0 °C throughout the melting process.

Key Fact

Specific heat capacity (SHC) — involves a temperature change, no state change: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). Specific latent heat (SLH) — involves a change of state at constant temperature: \(E = mL\). The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion.
exam_tip_html: The most common error in SHC calculations is using the total temperature rather than the change in temperature (\(\Delta\theta\)). Always subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature first. For latent heat questions, remember that temperature stays constant during a change of state — if a question asks you to calculate energy for melting or boiling, use \(E = mL\), not \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\) (there is no \(\Delta\theta\) term because temperature does not change). Make sure you state units in all final answers — J or kJ for energy.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy of all particles. Heating raises temperature (more kinetic energy) or causes a change of state (more potential energy at constant temperature). Heating curves show these as sloping sections and flat plateaus respectively.
  • Specific heat capacity (\(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C without changing state. Water’s high SHC (4200 J/(kg °C)) makes it useful for heating systems.
  • Specific latent heat (\(E = mL\)) is the energy for a change of state at constant temperature. Latent heat of vaporisation is always much greater than latent heat of fusion because more energy is needed to fully separate particles into a gas.

practice_questions.text:
What happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state, such as melting?
A) It rises steadily
B) It falls steadily
C) It stays constant
D) It rises then falls
practice_questions.marks: C) It stays constant [1 mark — all energy goes into changing potential energy, not kinetic energy, so temperature does not change]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, without a change of state (1). Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg at constant temperature, with no temperature change (1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat 3.0 kg of aluminium from 20 °C to 120 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: ΔE = mcΔθ (1). Correct temperature change: Δθ = 120 − 20 = 100 °C (1). Correct substitution: ΔE = 3.0 × 900 × 100 (1). Correct answer with unit: 270 000 J (or 270 kJ) (1). [4 marks — common errors: using 120 instead of 100 for Δθ; missing the unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the temperature stays constant during boiling, even though energy is being continuously supplied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During boiling, energy transferred to the liquid goes into increasing the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy; the particles need energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them and break away from the liquid; because kinetic energy does not increase, the average kinetic energy of the particles (and therefore the temperature) remains constant.
Secure: Energy going into potential energy (breaking bonds) rather than kinetic energy, linked to constant temperature.
Developing: States that energy is used for the change of state but does not mention kinetic/potential energy distinction.
Emerging: States temperature stays constant with no mechanism. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: How much energy is released when 2.0 kg of steam at 100 °C condenses to liquid water at 100 °C? The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2 260 000 J/kg. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation: E = mL (1). Correct substitution: E = 2.0 × 2 260 000 (1). Correct answer: 4 520 000 J (or 4520 kJ or 4.52 MJ) (1). Correct unit stated (1). Note: energy is released (not absorbed) during condensation — full marks if candidate notes the direction correctly. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student heats a block of iron using an electrical heater. The joulemeter shows 36 000 J of energy was supplied. The mass of the iron block is 2.0 kg and its temperature rose from 25 °C to 43 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of iron from this data.
practice_questions.marks: Correct equation rearranged: c = ΔE / (m × Δθ) (1). Correct temperature change: Δθ = 43 − 25 = 18 °C (1). Correct substitution: c = 36 000 / (2.0 × 18) = 36 000 / 36 (1). Correct answer with unit: 1000 J/(kg °C) (1). [4 marks — common errors: using 43 not 18 for Δθ; missing the unit; rearranging incorrectly]

knowledge_checks.q: Which equation is used to calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of a substance without a change of state?
Why is the specific latent heat of vaporisation always greater than the specific latent heat of fusion for the same substance?
options: Vaporisation happens at a higher temperature
More energy is needed to fully separate particles into a gas than to partially separate them into a liquid

knowledge_checks.q: During a change of state, the energy supplied increases the _____ energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy, so the temperature stays constant.
A heating curve shows flat sections (plateaus) at the melting point and boiling point, where the temperature remains constant while _____ of state occurs.
Match each quantity to its correct equation:
left: Energy for a change of state

flashcard_questions.a: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all particles in a substance.

flashcard_questions.q: State the equation for specific heat capacity calculations.
flashcard_questions.a: ΔE = mc Δθ (energy = mass × SHC × temperature change).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the specific heat capacity of water?
Why does water have a high specific heat capacity make it useful in central heating systems?
flashcard_questions.a: It can store a large amount of thermal energy per kilogram, releasing it slowly as it cools.

flashcard_questions.q: State the equation for specific latent heat.
flashcard_questions.a: E = mL (energy = mass × specific latent heat).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does temperature stay constant during a change of state?
flashcard_questions.a: Energy goes into changing potential energy (breaking intermolecular bonds), not kinetic energy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between the latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporisation?
flashcard_questions.a: Fusion is the energy to change from solid to liquid; vaporisation is solid to gas — vaporisation always requires more energy.

flashcard_questions.q: On a heating curve, what do the sloping sections represent?
flashcard_questions.a: Temperature rising — kinetic energy of particles increasing within a single state.

flashcard_questions.q: On a heating curve, what do the flat sections (plateaus) represent?
flashcard_questions.a: A change of state at constant temperature — potential energy of particles changing.

flashcard_questions.q: What is evaporation, and how does it differ from boiling?
flashcard_questions.a: Evaporation is surface loss of particles at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed boiling point.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the PAG associated with investigating specific heat capacity.
Why does evaporating liquid cause cooling of the remaining liquid?
flashcard_questions.a: The most energetic particles escape, lowering the average kinetic energy and therefore the temperature of the remaining liquid.

glossary_terms.definition: A change in the state of matter (such as melting or boiling) that can be reversed. The original properties of the substance are recovered when the change is reversed. No new substance is formed.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy stored by all the particles within a system.
A graph showing how the temperature of a substance changes as it is heated at a constant rate, including flat sections (plateaus) where changes of state occur at constant temperature.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K), without changing its state. Measured in J/(kg °C).
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature (no temperature change). Measured in J/kg.
